text: Winds on Neptune have been clocked at more than 2,000 km/h. That is faster than the [[@sky-sonic-boom|speed of sound]] on Earth, and about six times the top speed of Japan's [[@bullet-trains|bullet trains]]. No other planet's winds have been measured faster, though Saturn's come closest.

The strange part is that Neptune is the planet farthest from the Sun. It gets about 900 times less sunlight than Earth, and on Earth it is sunlight that drives the wind. Scientists think two things help. Neptune gives off more heat from deep inside than it receives from the Sun, which keeps its gases churning. And with no land or mountains to rub against, once the winds get going, very little slows them down.

st.prompt: Nobody saw Neptune until 1846. How did astronomers know where to point their telescope?

options.t: Maths showed something was tugging on Uranus
A sailor spotted it from a ship

st.reveal: Uranus was not moving quite where it should. Two mathematicians worked out that an unseen planet's gravity must be pulling it. On the first night of searching, an astronomer in Berlin found Neptune very close to the predicted spot.

n.certNote: The wind speeds are well measured. Why they are so fast is still being worked out. Heat from inside the planet and very little friction are the leading explanations.

The famous deep-blue pictures from Voyager 2 were colour-enhanced to bring out details. A 2024 study found that Neptune and Uranus are both a similar pale greenish blue, with Neptune only slightly bluer.

sec.t:
Neptune is the only planet found by maths before anyone saw it. In the early 1800s, [[astronomer|astronomers]] noticed that [[@uranus-sideways|Uranus]] kept drifting slightly off its predicted path. Something unseen seemed to be tugging it.

Using [[@newton-life|Newton's laws of gravity]], the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier calculated where a hidden planet should be. In England, John Couch Adams had been working on the same puzzle. On 23 September 1846, Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory looked where Le Verrier said, and found Neptune within an hour. For years afterwards, British and French astronomers argued over whether Adams or Le Verrier deserved the credit. Today both are usually named.

[[@galileo|Galileo]] had actually seen Neptune more than 200 years earlier, in 1612 and 1613. He drew it in his notes as a faint star.

The strongest [[@hurricanes|hurricanes]] and [[cyclone|cyclones]] on Earth have winds of around 300 km/h. Neptune's fastest winds are roughly seven times stronger. They blow mostly in bands around the planet, some heading the opposite way to Neptune's spin.

Neptune is about four times as wide as Earth and is an [[@space-weird-hot-ice|ice giant]], like Uranus. Below its clouds lies a deep, hot layer of water, ammonia and methane. Heat leaking out from that interior may be what keeps the weather so wild, even in the cold and dark of the outer [[solar-system|solar system]].

Neptune has at least 16 moons. The largest, Triton, travels around the planet in the opposite direction to Neptune's spin. No other big moon in the solar system does that.

The best explanation is that Triton did not form there. It was probably a small icy world, a bit like [[@pluto|Pluto]], that wandered too close and was captured by Neptune's [[gravity|gravity]]. Voyager 2 spotted dark plumes on Triton, possibly [[@geysers-hot-springs|geysers of nitrogen gas]], rising about 8 km above its frozen surface. Triton is one of the coldest places ever measured, at about −235°C.

Neptune's gravity is slowly dragging Triton closer. In a few billion years it may be pulled apart, and its pieces could spread out into a ring around the planet.

text: Scientists compare the animal very carefully with every similar species already known. They look at its body, bones, colours, sounds and, today, its [[dna|DNA]].

If it is clearly different, and the difference has built up over a long time, they publish a scientific description and give it a new two-part name. Only then is it officially a new [[species|species]].

quiz.prompt: Why might monkeys on opposite banks of a huge river slowly become different species?

options.t: They cannot cross, so each group changes in its own way over time
The water on each side makes them a different colour
They choose to stop talking to each other

quiz.reveal: Howler monkeys live in the treetops and do not swim across wide rivers. Over hundreds of thousands of years, small changes build up separately on each side. Eventually the two groups are different enough to count as separate species.

d.try: Collect leaves from two trees that look almost the same, perhaps two kinds of mango or ficus. Lay them side by side and list every difference you can find in shape, edges, veins and smell. This is what taxonomists do when they compare museum specimens.
myth: By now, scientists have found and named every kind of monkey and mammal on Earth.

New mammal species are still described every year, from bats and rodents to primates. Many look almost the same as known animals, so only careful study of DNA and skeletons reveals they are different.
facts: Every species gets a two-part Latin name, like Panthera tigris for the tiger

sec.t:
The [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon]] is crossed by giant rivers. Howler monkeys spend almost their whole lives high in the forest [[canopy|canopy]]. To them, a wide river is like a wall.

When a group of animals is cut off for a very long time, it slowly changes in its own way. Rivers have kept howler populations apart for millions of years, helping new species form. This is one reason [[@rainforests|rainforests]] are bursting with so many kinds of life. India's [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], full of separate hills and valleys, are another hotspot where new frogs, insects and plants are found every year.

Howler monkeys live in Central and South America. They eat mostly leaves and use their strong tail like a fifth hand. At dawn, males roar to tell other groups where they are. A hollow bone in the throat makes the sound boom for several kilometres, which puts howlers among the [[@extreme-loudest-animals|loudest animals]] on land.

Naming a species matters. Once it has a name, it can be counted, studied and protected. Scientists warn that the new howlers may already be at risk, because their forest [[habitat|habitat]] is being cleared for farms.

text: An ATM, or automated teller machine, is a computer in a strong steel box, connected to banks over a secure network. When you put in your card and type your PIN, the machine reads your card, scrambles your PIN and sends both to your [[@money-banks|bank]]. The bank's computer checks that the PIN is right and that there's enough money in your account.

If everything matches, the bank sends back a yes. The ATM counts out notes from locked boxes inside, pushes them out of the slot and records the withdrawal. Your bank balance drops at the same moment.
The whole conversation between machine and bank usually takes just a few seconds.

st.prompt: When you type your PIN at an ATM, where is it checked?

options.t: By your bank's computer, after the PIN is scrambled and sent over a network
Inside the plastic card itself, only
By a person watching on a camera

st.reveal: The machine scrambles your PIN with encryption and sends it, along with your card details, to your bank's computers. Many chip cards can also check the PIN on the chip. Either way, no human ever sees it.

myth: If you type your PIN backwards at an ATM, it secretly calls the police.

This story has spread by email and social media for years, but banks and police say no such system is in use. If you're ever threatened at a cash machine, the safest thing is to hand over the money and tell an adult or the police straight away.

sec.t:
The story goes that John Shepherd-Barron, a British engineer, got the idea in the bath after arriving at his bank just after it had closed. If chocolate bars could come out of a machine, he thought, why not cash?

His machine opened at a Barclays branch in Enfield, north London, on 27 June 1967. Customers bought special paper cheques in advance. Each carried a mark of carbon-14, a very faintly [[radioactive|radioactive]] substance, which the machine could detect. You put in the cheque, typed a number and got ten pounds.

Shepherd-Barron wanted a six-digit code, using his army number. His wife, Caroline, said she could only remember four. So four digits it was, and four-digit PINs are still the most common worldwide.

A modern ATM has a few main parts. A card reader takes information from the magnetic stripe or, more securely, the small gold chip. A keypad with a metal shield lets you type your PIN. A screen shows instructions.

Deep inside is a safe holding cash cassettes, boxes of notes sorted by value. A dispenser pulls notes out one at a time. [[sensor|Sensors]] measure each note's thickness with light, so two stuck together get rejected rather than handed out by mistake.

The PIN never travels as plain numbers. It's scrambled using [[@encryption|encryption]] before it leaves the keypad, so even if someone tapped the line, they'd see only gibberish.

{{story:upi-payments}}

India's first ATM was opened by HSBC in Mumbai in 1987. For years ATMs stayed mainly in big cities. Then banks spread them to towns and villages, and many now take cards from any Indian bank through shared networks.

By March 2025, India had about 2,51,000 ATMs, according to the Reserve Bank of India. That was slightly fewer than a year before, because more people now pay by phone using [[@upi-payments|UPI]] instead of carrying cash.

Indian ATMs can be found in surprising places, from railway stations and ferry jetties to towns high in the Himalayas. In the USA, many ATMs are owned by private companies and sit in petrol stations, shops and even bars, charging a fee for each withdrawal.

Thieves try tricks such as fake card readers stuck over the real slot, called skimmers, and tiny cameras aimed at the keypad. That's why banks tell customers to cover their hand while typing a PIN and to check that nothing looks loose or odd.

Chip cards help, because they're much harder to copy than magnetic stripes. Some new ATMs work with no card at all, by scanning a QR code with a phone.

As [[@passwords|passwords]] and phones take over, cash use is falling in many countries. But ATMs still matter for people without smartphones, or in places where the internet is patchy. The basic job hasn't changed since 1967: check who you are, check what you have, and count out notes without a single mistake.

text: A bullet train goes fast because almost everything about it is designed for speed. It runs on its own special tracks, with gentle curves, no level crossings and long, smooth welded rails. It is powered by electricity from overhead wires, with motors spread along many carriages rather than one big engine at the front. And its long, sleek nose slices through the air.

At high speed, air resistance is the main thing a train has to fight. Double the speed, and the air pushes back about four times as hard. So engineers shape the nose, smooth the sides and hide gaps between carriages. Japan's fastest Shinkansen trains now run at about 320 km/h, covering a [[@speed-distance|distance]] the length of a cricket pitch in about a quarter of a second.

st.prompt: Why did early Japanese bullet trains make a loud boom when they shot out of tunnels?

options.t: The train pushed a wave of squashed air ahead of it through the tunnel
The wheels hit a bump at the tunnel entrance
The engine backfired in the dark

st.reveal: A fast train enters a tunnel like a plunger into a syringe, squeezing the air ahead of it. That pressure wave bursts out of the far end with a bang. A long, slim, beak-shaped nose lets the air flow around the train more gently and makes the boom much quieter.

sec.t:
In 1964, [[@tokyo|Tokyo]] was getting ready to host the [[@olympics|Olympic Games]]. Just nine days before they began, on 1 October, Japan opened the Tokaido Shinkansen, a new railway linking Tokyo and Osaka. Its trains reached 210 km/h, faster than any passenger train in regular service had gone before. People called them "bullet trains" because of their rounded noses and speed.

The idea spread. France opened its TGV in 1981. China began building high-speed lines in the 2000s, and it now has the largest network in the world, more than 40,000 kilometres.

A [[@maglev|maglev train]] doesn't touch the track at all. Powerful [[@magnets-how|magnets]] lift it a few centimetres into the air and push it forward, so there are no wheels to rub. In 2015, Japan's test maglev reached 603 km/h. Shanghai has run a maglev line to its airport since 2004.

Maglevs are very expensive to build, though, because they need completely new tracks. So most of the world's high-speed trains still use steel wheels on rails, just better rails, better wheels and better shapes than ordinary trains.

India is building its first high-speed line, between Mumbai and Ahmedabad. It will be about 500 kilometres long and is being built with Japanese help, using Shinkansen technology. Part of it will run through a tunnel under the sea near Thane Creek. When finished, trains are expected to cover the distance in around two to three hours, compared with about five to seven hours on regular trains now.

Bullet trains also have to be extremely safe. In Japan, [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] [[sensor|sensors]] along the line can cut the power and brake trains within seconds of the first tremor. That's part of why, in more than 60 years, no passenger has died in a Shinkansen crash or derailment.

text: [[@how-fridges-cold|A fridge]] is a heat mover. Inside its walls, a special liquid called a [[refrigerant|refrigerant]] flows round and round through thin pipes. When the refrigerant [[evaporation|evaporates]], turning from liquid to gas in the coils inside the fridge, it soaks up heat from the food and air around it. That's why the inside gets cold.

The gas then flows to a pump called a compressor, usually the humming box at the bottom of the fridge. The compressor squeezes the gas hard, which makes it hot. The hot gas flows through coils at the back or sides of the fridge, where it gives its heat to the kitchen air and turns back into a liquid. Then it squeezes through a very narrow valve, cools sharply, and goes back inside to soak up more heat. Round and round, all day and night.

st.prompt: On a hot day, you leave the fridge door open to cool the kitchen. What happens to the room?

options.t: It cools down a little
It gets slightly warmer
Nothing changes

st.reveal: The fridge just moves heat from inside the box to the coils at the back, which are in the same room. Its motor also gives off heat. So with the door open, it pumps heat round in a circle and adds a bit more. The room ends up warmer, not cooler.

sec.t:
You already know the trick behind a fridge. When you climb out of a swimming pool on a windy day, you shiver, even in summer. As water evaporates from your skin, it carries heat away with it. Your body uses the same idea when it [[@sweat|sweats]].

In India, a clay *matka* or *surahi* keeps [[@water-drink|drinking water]] cool for the same reason. Water seeps slowly through the tiny holes in the clay and evaporates from the outside of the pot, taking heat with it. A fridge does the same thing, but in a sealed loop, using a liquid that evaporates far more easily than water.

During the 1800s, inventors in the USA and Europe built machines that made cold using evaporating liquids and compressors. At first they were huge and used for breweries, meat packers and ships. By the 1920s and 1930s, electric fridges small enough for a kitchen were spreading in American homes. In India, fridges became common in middle-class homes much later, in the decades after the 1980s.

Fridges changed what people eat. Milk, meat, vegetables and leftovers could last for days instead of hours. Cooking and shopping changed too, since families no longer needed to buy fresh food every day.

For decades, many fridges used gases called CFCs. They were safe and did not burn, but when old fridges leaked or were thrown away, the gases drifted high into the sky. There they damaged the [[@ozone-layer|ozone layer]], which shields Earth from harmful sunlight.

In 1987, countries signed the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to phase out these gases. Modern fridges use different refrigerants, and the [[ozone|ozone]] layer is slowly healing. Some of the newer gases still trap heat and warm the planet, so engineers keep looking for better ones, including gases as simple as the propane-like isobutane found in many new fridges.

text: पुरानी पेंटिंगें गंदी और खराब हो जाती हैं। धुआँ, धूल और उँगलियों के निशान उन पर जम जाते हैं। वार्निश, यानी वह पारदर्शी बचाव परत जिसे कलाकार ऊपर से लगाते थे, हवा के असर से धीरे-धीरे पीली या भूरी पड़ जाती है। यह उसी तरह का धीमा रासायनिक बदलाव है जिससे लोहे पर [[@rust|ज़ंग]] लगता है, यानी [[oxidation|ऑक्सीकरण]]। रंग चटक सकता है, पपड़ी बनकर झड़ सकता है या फीका पड़ सकता है।

जानकार, जिन्हें [[conservator|संरक्षक]] कहते हैं, पेंटिंगों को साफ़ करते और उनकी मरम्मत करते हैं, ताकि वे टिकी रहें और वैसी दिखें जैसा कलाकार चाहता था। वे धीरे-धीरे काम करते हैं, अक्सर रुई के फाहों, हल्के तरलों और माइक्रोस्कोप से। कुछ भी छूने से पहले वे एक्स-रे, इन्फ़्रारेड कैमरों और रंग के नन्हे नमूनों से पेंटिंग की जाँच करते हैं। और वे एक सुनहरा नियम मानते हैं: जो कुछ भी वे जोड़ें, उसे आगे चलकर कोई हटा सके।

sec.t:
संरक्षक बहुत पास से देखकर शुरुआत करता है। माइक्रोस्कोप में एक दरार किसी घाटी जैसी लग सकती है। [[ultraviolet|पराबैंगनी]] रोशनी में पुराना वार्निश हरा-सा चमकता है, जबकि बाद की मरम्मत गहरे धब्बों जैसी दिखती है।

[[@x-rays|एक्स-रे]] कुछ रंगों के आर-पार निकल जाते हैं और कुछ के नहीं। इससे छिपे हुए बदलाव सामने आ सकते हैं। पिकासो की पेंटिंग *द ब्लू रूम* में जाँच से नीचे एक दाढ़ी वाले आदमी का चित्र मिला। इन्फ़्रारेड कैमरे रंग के नीचे कलाकार की पहली रेखाएँ देख सकते हैं, वैसे ही जैसे साफ़-सुथरे निबंध के नीचे उसका कच्चा मसौदा दिख जाए।

sec.h: वह रात जो असल में दिन थी
sec.t:
रेम्ब्रांट ने 1642 में एम्स्टर्डम के नगर-रक्षकों का अपना विशाल सामूहिक चित्र बनाया। समय के साथ वार्निश और मैल की परतों ने उसे इतना काला कर दिया कि लोग उसे *द नाइट वॉच*, यानी रात का पहरा, कहने लगे। 1940 के दशक की सफ़ाई के बाद पता चला कि दृश्य दिन का है, पर नाम चलता रहा।

2019 में रेक्सम्यूज़ियम ने ऑपरेशन नाइट वॉच शुरू किया। संरक्षकों ने दीर्घा के भीतर एक शीशे के कमरे में काम किया, ताकि लोग देख सकें। उन्होंने 8,000 से ज़्यादा बेहद बारीक तस्वीरें खींचीं, उन्हें जोड़कर एक विशाल तस्वीर बनाई, और रंग की हर परत का नक्शा तैयार किया।

1980 से 1994 के बीच रोम के सिस्टीन चैपल में [[@michelangelo|माइकलएंजेलो]] की छत और दीवारों के चित्र साफ़ किए गए। सदियों का मोमबत्ती का धुआँ और पुराना गोंद हटाया गया। नीचे चटक नारंगी, हरे और गुलाबी रंग निकले।

कुछ कला-जानकार खुशी से उछल पड़े। दूसरों का कहना था कि सफ़ाई ने मैल के साथ माइकलएंजेलो की अपनी आखिरी छायाएँ भी मिटा दीं। यह बहस दिखाती है कि कला की मरम्मत में हमेशा कठिन फ़ैसले करने पड़ते हैं।

भारत में [[@ajanta-colours|अजंता]] के 1,500 साल पुराने गुफ़ा-चित्रों का इतिहास पेचीदा रहा है। 1920 के दशक में मरम्मत करने वालों ने उन्हें बचाने के लिए कुछ हिस्सों पर लाख (शेलैक) का वार्निश चढ़ा दिया। समय के साथ वह काला और पीला पड़ गया, और उन्हीं रंगों को छिपा बैठा जिन्हें बचाना था।

बाद में भारतीय पुरातत्व सर्वेक्षण के संरक्षकों ने बरसों लगाकर वह वार्निश धीरे-धीरे हटाया। आज वे रोशनी और [[humidity|नमी]] पर काबू रखते हैं, और कुछ गुफ़ाओं में एक साथ जाने वाले लोगों की गिनती सीमित रखते हैं, क्योंकि इंसान की साँस में नमी होती है जो रंग को नुकसान पहुँचा सकती है।

2012 में स्पेन के बोर्खा कस्बे में एक बुज़ुर्ग शौकिया चित्रकार ने चर्च में ईसा मसीह की एक झड़ती पेंटिंग ठीक करने की कोशिश की। उनका बनाया रूप किसी रोएँदार बंदर जैसा ज़्यादा लगा। तस्वीरें दुनिया भर में फैल गईं। तब से सैलानी बड़ी तादाद में उस चर्च को देखने आते हैं, और कस्बे ने यादगार चीज़ें तक बेची हैं।

इसीलिए संग्रहालय प्रशिक्षित संरक्षकों पर भरोसा करते हैं। वही जाँचें और रंग के परीक्षण कभी-कभी एक अलग ही राज़ खोल देते हैं: एक ऐसी पेंटिंग जो पुरानी है ही नहीं, बल्कि [[@art-forgery|कला की जालसाज़ी]] का एक चालाक नमूना है।

text: ढोकरा, जिसे डोकरा भी लिखते हैं, लुप्त मोम विधि से धातु की मूर्तियाँ बनाने का एक तरीका है। कलाकार मिट्टी के भीतरी ढाँचे पर मोम से नमूना बनाता है, उस पर और मिट्टी चढ़ाता है, फिर उसे गर्म करता है ताकि मोम पिघलकर बह जाए। मोम की छोड़ी हुई ख़ाली जगह में पिघला पीतल डाला जाता है। ठंडा होने पर मिट्टी तोड़ दी जाती है, और धातु की मूर्ति निकल आती है।
यह दुनिया के सबसे पुराने धातु-ढलाई के तरीकों में से एक है। भारत में इसे मुख्य रूप से छत्तीसगढ़, पश्चिम बंगाल, ओडिशा, झारखंड और आसपास के राज्यों के [[indigenous|आदिवासी]] और ग्रामीण समुदाय करते हैं।
ढोकरा की चीज़ें आसानी से पहचानी जाती हैं: घोड़े, हाथी, उल्लू, आदिवासी देवी-देवता, दीये और नर्तक, जिन पर अक्सर बटे हुए धागे जैसी बारीक उभरी लकीरें होती हैं।

sec.t:
1926 में [[@indus-cities|सिंधु घाटी के बड़े शहरों]] में से एक, मोहनजोदड़ो, में [[archaeologist|पुरातत्वविदों]] को लगभग 10 सेंटीमीटर ऊँची एक लड़की की काँसे की छोटी मूर्ति मिली। वह एक हाथ कमर पर रखे खड़ी है, और उसकी बाँह चूड़ियों से भरी है। वह लगभग 4,500 साल पुरानी है और लुप्त मोम विधि से बनी थी।

आज उसे नाचती लड़की (डांसिंग गर्ल) के नाम से जाना जाता है, और वह नई दिल्ली के राष्ट्रीय संग्रहालय के ख़ज़ानों में से एक है। ढोकरा कलाकार 4,000 से ज़्यादा साल बाद भी लगभग उसी ढंग से काम करने वाला तरीका अपनाते हैं।

ढोकरा नाम को अक्सर पूर्वी भारत के घुमंतू धातु-कारीगरों, ढोकरा डामर, से जोड़ा जाता है।

पहले कलाकार धान की भूसी मिली मिट्टी से एक मोटा भीतरी ढाँचा बनाकर सूखने देता है। फिर आता है मोम, आम तौर पर आसपास के छत्तों का मधुमक्खी का मोम, जिसमें पेड़ की राल मिलाई जाती है। उसे नरम करके छलनी जैसे एक औज़ार से दबाकर पतले धागों में निकाला जाता है और ढाँचे पर लपेटा जाता है। नमूने, आँखें और गहने भी मोम से ही जोड़े जाते हैं।

इसके बाद मोम के नमूने पर पहले महीन मिट्टी की और फिर मोटी मिट्टी की परतें चढ़ाई जाती हैं, और एक छोटी नाली खुली छोड़ी जाती है। सूखने पर साँचा आग में रखा जाता है। मोम पिघलकर बह जाता है, इसीलिए इसे "लुप्त मोम" कहते हैं।

इस बीच मिट्टी की कुठाली में पीतल पिघलाया जाता है। उसे नाली से गर्म साँचे में डाला जाता है, और वह मोम के छोड़े हर धागे और हर घुमाव को भर देता है। ठंडा होने पर मिट्टी तोड़कर खोली जाती है, और चीज़ को साफ़ करके चमकाया जाता है।

आज ज़्यादातर ढोकरा पीतल से बनता है, जो ताँबे और जस्ते की एक [[alloy|मिश्रधातु]] है। कलाकार अक्सर पीतल के पुराने बर्तन, टूटे दीये और कबाड़ पिघला लेते हैं। इस हिसाब से ढोकरा हमेशा से एक तरह का [[@recycling|रीसाइक्लिंग]] रहा है।

[[@honey|मधुमक्खी का मोम]] भी दोबारा काम आता है। जब वह साँचे से बहकर निकलता है, तो उसका कुछ हिस्सा जमा करके फिर इस्तेमाल किया जा सकता है।

छत्तीसगढ़ के बस्तर में कोंडागाँव ढोकरा का एक मशहूर केंद्र है। पश्चिम बंगाल में बाँकुड़ा के पास बिकना और बर्धमान के दरियापुर के कलाकार इस कला के लिए जाने जाते हैं। ढोकरा [[@odisha|ओडिशा]], झारखंड और मध्य प्रदेश में भी बनता है।

बस्तर ढोकरा और बंगाल डोकरा, दोनों को भौगोलिक संकेत यानी जीआई टैग मिला है। जीआई टैग एक तरह का सरकारी ठप्पा है, जो बताता है कि कोई चीज़ सचमुच किसी ख़ास जगह से आती है।

सदियों तक ढोकरा कारीगर स्थानीय इस्तेमाल के लिए दीये, अनाज नापने के कटोरे, पायल और गाँव के देवताओं की मूर्तियाँ बनाते रहे। अब उनका काम दस्तकारी मेलों, शहरों की दुकानों और विदेशों में बिकता है। कुछ कलाकार पारंपरिक घोड़ों और हाथियों के साथ-साथ पेन-स्टैंड और दीवार पर टाँगने वाली सजावट जैसे नए डिज़ाइन भी बनाते हैं।

काम गर्म, धीमा और कठिन है, और कुछ गाँवों के नौजवान दूसरे काम चुन रहे हैं। दस्तकारी संगठन और सरकारी योजनाएँ कलाकारों को ख़रीदार और सही दाम दिलाने की कोशिश करती हैं, ताकि हर नई चीज़, जो एक बार बनती है और फिर कभी नहीं, 4,500 साल पुराने एक विचार को ज़िंदा रखे।

text: वोल्फ़गैंग अमाडेयस मोत्ज़ार्ट ऑस्ट्रिया के संगीतकार थे, जो 1756 से 1791 तक जिए। वे इतिहास के सबसे मशहूर बाल कलाकारों में से एक थे, जो छह साल की उम्र से यूरोप भर में घूम-घूमकर प्रस्तुतियाँ देते थे। बड़े होकर उन्होंने लगभग हर तरह का संगीत रचा: सिम्फ़नी, [[@opera|ऑपेरा]], पियानो कॉन्सर्टो, चर्च संगीत, और छोटी मंडलियों के लिए रचनाएँ।

सिर्फ़ 35 सालों में उन्होंने 600 से ज़्यादा रचनाएँ लिखीं। इनमें से बहुत-सी आज भी पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत की सबसे ज़्यादा बजाई जाने वाली रचनाओं में हैं। लोग उनके संगीत को उसकी साफ़ धुनों और चुस्त [[rhythm|लय]], उसकी चंचलता, और अचानक गंभीर या उदास हो जाने के अंदाज़ के लिए पसंद करते हैं। *द मैजिक फ़्लूट* जैसे उनके ऑपेरा दुनिया भर में खेले जाते हैं।

sec.t:
1770 में मोत्ज़ार्ट परिवार रोम गया। [[@michelangelo|सिस्टीन चैपल]] में उन्होंने ग्रेगोरियो अल्लेग्री की रचना *मिज़ेरेरे* सुनी, जिसे [[@vatican|वेटिकन]] का [[@choirs|गायक-दल]] सिर्फ़ ईस्टर से पहले के पवित्र सप्ताह में गाता था। इसकी हस्तलिखित प्रतियाँ, यानी [[manuscript|पांडुलिपियाँ]], चैपल से बाहर ले जाने की मनाही थी।

पिता की चिट्ठियों के मुताबिक 14 साल के वोल्फ़गैंग ने इसे सुनने के बाद पूरी रचना याद से लिख डाली, और फिर जाँचने के लिए दोबारा सुनने गए। ऐसे किस्सों से वे लगभग जादुई लगते थे। आज के वैज्ञानिक कहते हैं कि ऐसा हुनर बहुत छोटी उम्र से ढेर सारे अभ्यास से आता है। इस तरह साधा गया दिमाग संगीत में बहुत माहिर हो जाता है, जैसा तुम [[@brain-works|दिमाग कैसे काम करता है]] में पढ़ सकते हो।

जवानी में मोत्ज़ार्ट साल्ज़बर्ग के आर्चबिशप के यहाँ नौकरी करते थे, पर उन्हें नौकर जैसा बर्ताव बिल्कुल नहीं भाता था। 1781 में वे नौकरी छोड़कर विएना चले गए, ताकि सिखाकर, प्रस्तुतियाँ देकर और अपना संगीत बेचकर गुज़ारा कर सकें। उस ज़माने में यह अनोखा और जोखिम भरा कदम था।

विएना में उन्होंने अपनी कई सबसे महान रचनाएँ लिखीं, जिनमें वे पियानो कॉन्सर्टो भी हैं जिन्हें वे अपने ज़माने के [[@piano|पियानो]] पर खुद बजाते थे। फिर आए उनके ऑपेरा *द मैरिज ऑफ़ फ़िगारो* और *डॉन जियोवानी*। कभी-कभी वे अच्छा कमा लेते थे, पर खुले हाथ से खर्च भी करते थे और अक्सर उधार लेना पड़ता था।

1791 में उनका ऑपेरा *द मैजिक फ़्लूट* विएना में कामयाब रहा। इसमें 'रात की रानी' का जोशीला गीत है, जो सोप्रानो (सबसे ऊँची स्त्री आवाज़) के लिए सबसे मुश्किल रचनाओं में से एक है। इसके [[pitch|सुर]] ज़्यादातर आवाज़ों की पहुँच से बहुत ऊपर हैं, जैसा [[@singing|गायन]] में समझाया गया है।

बीमार पड़ने के समय वे एक रेक्विएम भी लिख रहे थे, यानी मृतकों की याद में गाया जाने वाला संगीत। 5 दिसंबर 1791 को 35 साल की उम्र में उनका निधन हो गया। रेक्विएम उनके एक शिष्य ने पूरा किया।

1984 की फ़िल्म *अमाडेयस* में एक प्रतिद्वंद्वी संगीतकार, अंतोनियो सालिएरी, को मोत्ज़ार्ट के खिलाफ़ साज़िश रचते दिखाया गया। कहानी शानदार है, पर इतिहासकारों को कोई सबूत नहीं मिला कि सालिएरी ने उन्हें कोई नुकसान पहुँचाया। दोनों एक-दूसरे को जानते थे और लगता है कि वे शिष्ट प्रतिद्वंद्वी थे।

एक और भ्रम यह है कि बच्चों को मोत्ज़ार्ट सुनाने से वे ज़्यादा होशियार हो जाते हैं। 1993 के एक छोटे-से अध्ययन से यह विचार फैला, पर बाद के शोध में कोई टिकाऊ असर नहीं मिला। युवा संगीतकार [[@beethoven|बीथोवन]] शायद 1787 में मोत्ज़ार्ट से मिलने की उम्मीद में विएना आए थे। अगर वे मिले, तो क्या हुआ, यह पक्के तौर पर कोई नहीं जानता।

text: लय का मतलब है कि आवाज़ें समय में कैसे सजी हैं। ज़्यादातर संगीत के नीचे एक थाप चलती रहती है, घड़ी की टिक-टिक जैसी एक-सी धड़कन, जिस पर तुम पैर थपथपाते हो। उस थाप के ऊपर लंबी और छोटी आवाज़ों और चुप्पियों का जो पैटर्न बिछता है, वही [[rhythm|लय]] है।

क्रिकेट स्टेडियम में नारे लगाती भीड़ के बारे में सोचो। थाप है तालियों की एक-सी धमक। लय है उसके ऊपर बोले जाने वाले शब्दों का पैटर्न: कुछ फटाफट, कुछ खिंचे हुए, कुछ तालियों के बीच में पड़ते हुए। रफ़्तार भी मायने रखती है। संगीतकार इसे गति या टेम्पो कहते हैं और प्रति मिनट थापों में नापते हैं।

sec.t:
1815 में योहान मेल्ज़ेल ने मेट्रोनोम का पेटेंट कराया। यह टिक-टिक करने वाली एक मशीन है, जिसमें [[pendulum|लोलक]] जैसी एक झूलती डंडी होती है और जिसे किसी भी रफ़्तार पर सेट किया जा सकता है। [[@beethoven|बेथोवन]] उन पहले संगीतकारों में थे जिन्होंने अपने संगीत पर मेट्रोनोम की रफ़्तार लिखी।

आज संगीतकार मेट्रोनोम वाले ऐप इस्तेमाल करते हैं। कोई धीमी रचना 60 थाप प्रति मिनट की हो सकती है, यानी हर सेकंड एक। कोई तेज़ डांस गाना 130 या उससे भी ज़्यादा का हो सकता है। आराम करते समय तुम्हारा दिल मिनट में लगभग 60 से 100 बार धड़कता है, और दौड़ने पर तेज़ हो जाता है, जैसा [[@heartbeat-exercise|तुम्हारी धड़कन]] में बताया गया है। कुछ लोगों को पैदल चलने की रफ़्तार के आसपास वाले संगीत पर थिरकना ख़ास तौर पर आसान लगता है।

कुछ सबसे रोमांचक लयें थाप पर नहीं, उसके ख़िलाफ़ चलती हैं। इसे सिंकोपेशन कहते हैं। कोई सुर ठीक वहाँ से ज़रा पहले या ज़रा बाद पड़ता है जहाँ तुम उसकी उम्मीद कर रहे थे, और इससे हैरानी का एक छोटा-सा झटका लगता है।

[[@jazz|जैज़]] सिंकोपेशन से भरा है, और लैटिन अमेरिकी डांस संगीत, [[@bhangra|भांगड़ा]] और हिप-हॉप भी। पश्चिमी अफ़्रीका के ढोल वादन में अक्सर कई ढोलची एक साथ अलग-अलग लयें बजाते हैं, जैसे दो-दो के गुच्छों के ख़िलाफ़ तीन-तीन के गुच्छे। इसे पॉलीरिदम कहते हैं। हर ढोलची को अपना हिस्सा थामे रखना पड़ता है, जबकि बाकी अलग-अलग दिशाओं में खींचते रहते हैं।

भारतीय संगीतकार लय को बोलकर सीखते हैं। दक्षिण भारत में *कोन्नकोल* की कला में लयों को "त क दि मि" जैसे [[syllable|अक्षरों]] में बदल दिया जाता है। तबला वादक ढोल छूने से पहले ही हर चोट को बोले जाने वाले *बोल* के रूप में सीखते हैं, जैसे "धा धिन धिन धा", जैसा [[@tabla|तबला]] में बताया गया है।

लय को बोलने से [[@brain-works|दिमाग़]] को उसे याद रखने में मदद मिलती है, ठीक वैसे जैसे तुकबंदी से कविता याद रहती है। रैपर भी कुछ ऐसा ही करते हैं। वे शब्दों को ऐसे ठूँसते हैं कि उनके अक्षर थापों पर और उनके बीच में पड़ें।

बहुत समय तक वैज्ञानिक मानते रहे कि संगीत के साथ ताल मिलाकर सिर्फ़ इंसान ही हिल सकते हैं। फिर 2009 में अमेरिका की एक टीम ने स्नोबॉल नाम के एक काकातुआ का अध्ययन किया। उन्होंने उसे एक ही गाना अलग-अलग रफ़्तार पर सुनाया। अक्सर वह उसी हिसाब से अपना सिर हिलाना और पैर उठाना तेज़ या धीमा कर लेता था।

दूसरे अध्ययनों में पाया गया कि तोते, और रोनन नाम का एक सी-लायन, थाप पकड़ सकते हैं। ये सब नई आवाज़ें या हरकतें सीखने में माहिर हैं। कुत्ते और बिल्लियाँ, कितने भी प्यारे हों, सावधानी से किए गए परीक्षणों में अब तक यह हुनर नहीं दिखा पाए हैं।

text: Mother Teresa was a Catholic nun who spent her life caring for the sick, the dying and the very poor in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]]. She was born in Europe in 1910, came to India as a young teacher, and in 1950 started a group of nuns called the Missionaries of Charity.
Her sisters ran homes for people who had nowhere else to go, including those with leprosy and the dying. The group spread to more than 100 countries.
She won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 1979 and India's highest civilian award, the Bharat Ratna, in 1980. After her death, the Catholic Church named her a saint.

sec.t:
She was born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje, to an Albanian family. At 18 she joined the Sisters of Loreto, an order of Irish nuns, and took the name Teresa.

In 1929 she arrived in India. For almost 20 years she taught at a girls' school in Kolkata, then called Calcutta, and became its head. Outside the school walls, the city was struggling with [[famine|famine]], and later with the violence and [[refugee|refugees]] of [[@partition|Partition]].

In 1952 she opened Nirmal Hriday, a home for dying people, beside the Kalighat temple. People found on the street were brought in, washed, fed and allowed to die with someone holding their hand.

Her sisters later opened homes for children, people with leprosy and the [[@pensions-old-age|elderly]]. When she died in 1997, India gave her a state funeral. In 2016, Pope Francis declared her Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

In 1950, the Church allowed her to start her own order, the Missionaries of Charity. Its first members were mostly her former pupils. Besides the usual vows of nuns, they promised "wholehearted and free service to the poorest of the poor".

The sisters lived simply. They owned a few saris, a bucket for washing and little else, and they went out each day to find people in need. The headquarters, called Mother House, still stands on a busy road in central Kolkata.

The order grew fast. By the time of her death, thousands of sisters and brothers were working in more than 100 countries, running soup kitchens, orphanages and homes for people with HIV. Many volunteers from around the world, including students, still come to Kolkata to help in the homes for a few weeks.

To millions, she was a symbol of selfless care. Yet her work also drew real criticism. Some doctors and journalists said her homes gave poor medical care and too little pain relief, even when money was available.

Others objected to her strong views against abortion and birth control, or to donations she accepted. Some in India worried that her work aimed at religious conversion, which her supporters denied. Like many famous people, she is remembered in more than one way, and readers can weigh the evidence for themselves.

text: Logic is the study of good reasoning. It asks a simple question: if these things are true, what else must be true? A logical argument starts from statements, called premises, and moves step by step to a conclusion.

Here is a famous example. All humans are mortal. [[@socrates|Socrates]] is a human. So Socrates is mortal. If the first two statements are true, the third cannot be false. Logic helps us spot when an argument works like that, and when it only seems to. It is used by mathematicians, lawyers, scientists, detectives and, above all, by [[@computers-how|computers]].

sec.t:
In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], about 2,350 years ago, the philosopher Aristotle studied arguments like the one about Socrates. He called them syllogisms and sorted them into patterns that always work and patterns that do not. His ideas were taught in Europe and the Middle East for nearly 2,000 years.

In India, a school of thought called Nyaya developed its own rules of reasoning and debate. They were written down in the *Nyaya Sutras* roughly 2,000 years ago, though scholars argue about the exact date. A Nyaya argument has five steps. Its favourite example: the hill has fire, because it has smoke, and wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen. Nyaya thinkers also listed the mistakes people make in arguments, much as modern books on critical thinking do.

Some arguments sound right but are broken. "If it rains, the road is wet. The road is wet, so it rained." That does not follow, because the road could be wet for other reasons. Another trap is assuming that because one thing happened after another, the first caused the second. You wore your lucky socks and your team won, but the socks probably had nothing to do with it.

A third trap is the false choice: "Either you love cricket or you hate sport." Plenty of people fall somewhere in between, or love football instead. Arguments like this hide all the other possibilities.

Spotting these traps is a useful skill when reading the news or scrolling online. Many false stories rely on arguments that only look logical, which is one reason people who study [[@fake-news|fake news]] teach logic.

{{story:computers-how}}

In 1854, an English schoolteacher turned professor named George Boole published *The Laws of Thought*. He showed that reasoning could be written like [[@algebra|algebra]], using just two values: true and false. He used three main operations: AND, OR and NOT.

"AND" is true only if both parts are true. "OR" is true if at least one part is. "NOT" flips true to false and false to true. Boole thought he was describing how the mind works. He had no idea he was writing the instruction manual for machines that did not exist yet.

In 1937, a young American student named Claude Shannon noticed that electric switches behave like Boole's logic. A switch is on or off, just like true or false. Two switches in a row act like AND, because current flows only if both are on. Two side by side act like OR.

Every computer chip today contains billions of tiny switches called [[@minecraft-coding|logic gates]], wired to follow Boole's rules. They work with 1 for true and 0 for false, the language of [[@binary-code|binary code]]. When you search [[@internet-how|the internet]], send a message or play a game, millions of AND, OR and NOT decisions are happening every second.

text: Cricket is a game of numbers, and fans remember records the way other people remember birthdays. The most famous include Don Bradman's Test [[@maths-sports-stats|batting average]] of 99.94, Brian Lara's 400 not out, Sachin Tendulkar's 100 international centuries and Muttiah Muralitharan's 800 Test wickets.

Some records feel almost impossible to beat. Others fall every few years as the game changes. One-day and T20 cricket, with their fast scoring, have produced a flood of new ones. That is part of the fun: a record set today might be broken by a teenager who is practising right now.

sec.t:
Don Bradman of Australia played 52 Tests between 1928 and 1948. He scored 6,996 runs and was out 70 times, giving a batting [[@averages|average]] of 99.94. Most great batters average about 50 to 60. Bradman's number is so far ahead that statisticians say no record in any major sport is quite like it.

He needed just four runs in his last innings to reach 100. The crowd at The Oval stood and cheered him, the England players gave him three cheers, and he was bowled second ball for nought. Some people think the emotion of the moment got to him.

A team has ten wickets in an innings, and taking all of them alone is extremely rare in Tests. Only three bowlers have done it. Jim Laker of England took 10 for 53 against Australia in 1956, and 19 wickets in the match. Anil Kumble took 10 for 74 against Pakistan in Delhi in 1999.

The third story is the strangest. In December 2021, Ajaz Patel took all ten Indian wickets for New Zealand at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai. Ajaz had been born in Mumbai and moved to New Zealand as a child, so he did it in his own birth city.

[[@sachin-tendulkar|Sachin Tendulkar]] played 200 Tests, scored 15,921 Test runs and made 100 international centuries, all records. In 2023 [[@virat-kohli|Virat Kohli]] passed Sachin's 49 one-day hundreds with his 50th, in a World Cup semi-final in the same Mumbai stadium. Sachin was watching.

Muttiah Muralitharan of Sri Lanka took exactly 800 Test wickets, the last with the final ball he bowled in Tests, in 2010. The fastest bowlers rarely play as long, because bowling fast is hard on the body.

Six sixes in an over has been hit in international cricket only a handful of times. Yuvraj Singh did it against England's Stuart Broad at the 2007 T20 World Cup in Durban. The first to do it in any first-class match was Garfield Sobers, in 1968.

Records keep changing, so cricket websites update them daily. Some numbers, like Bradman's, may never be beaten. That is why fans still argue about them in buses, trains and school canteens.

text: Onam and Pongal are harvest festivals from South India. Onam is celebrated in Kerala in August or September, at the end of the [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains. Pongal is celebrated in Tamil Nadu in mid-January, after the rice harvest. Both are times for new clothes, family feasts and giving thanks for good crops.

Each has its own customs. Onam brings flower carpets, a giant vegetarian feast and [[@india-wonder-onam-boat-race|snake boat races]]. Pongal is named after a sweet rice dish boiled until it overflows, and one of its days honours the cattle that help on farms.

sec.t:
The best-known Onam story is about Mahabali, a generous asura king who ruled Kerala in a golden age when everyone was equal and no one went hungry. The gods grew worried about his power. Vishnu came as Vamana, a small boy-priest, and asked the king for as much land as he could cover in three steps.

Mahabali agreed. Vamana grew enormous. His first two steps covered the earth and the sky, and for the third, Mahabali offered his own head and was pushed down to the underworld. Because he was so loved, he was allowed to visit his people once a year. Onam is his homecoming.

Pongal falls in the Tamil month of Thai, on the same day as Makar Sankranti in much of India, when people elsewhere [[@kites-festival|fly kites]]. It lasts four days.

On Bhogi, the first day, families clear out old things and clean their homes. Thai Pongal, the main day, is when the new rice is cooked with milk and [[@jaggery|jaggery]] in a clay or brass pot, outside in the sun, until it bubbles over. The overflow is a sign of plenty. The word "pongal" itself means "[[@boiling-water|boiling]] over".

The third day, Mattu Pongal, honours cattle. Cows and bulls are washed, their horns are painted and decorated with bells and flowers, and they are fed sweet pongal. Farmers thank them for ploughing fields and giving milk.

In some villages, this is also when jallikattu is held, a sport in which young men try to hold on to a running bull. It has been the subject of long court cases over animal welfare. The Supreme Court allowed it to continue in 2023 under rules set by the state. The fourth day, Kaanum Pongal, is for visiting relatives and going on outings.

In Tamil Nadu, women draw kolam at the doorstep every morning with rice flour, and the designs grow bigger and more colourful at Pongal. These patterns of dots and loops follow careful rules of [[symmetry|symmetry]], as [[@rangoli-symmetry|rangoli and symmetry]] shows.

Because they are made of rice flour, kolams also feed ants and small birds during the day. By evening they are often half eaten, and the next morning a new one begins.

टीके में कुछ ऐसा होता है जो कीटाणु जैसा दिखता है, पर तुम्हें बीमार नहीं कर सकता। यह कमज़ोर या मरा हुआ कीटाणु हो सकता है, उसके बाहरी खोल का बस एक टुकड़ा, या ऐसे निर्देश जिनसे तुम्हारी अपनी कोशिकाएँ थोड़ी देर के लिए वह टुकड़ा बना लें। शरीर उसे परखता है, [[antibody|एंटीबॉडी]] बनाता है, और [[@memory|याद]] रखने वाली कोशिकाएँ सँभालकर रखता है। अगर असली कीटाणु कभी आता है, तो शरीर उसे पहचान लेता है और फटाफट जवाबी हमला करता है, अक्सर तुम्हें कुछ महसूस होने से पहले ही।

1700 के दशक में चेचक बहुत बड़ी गिनती में लोगों की जान ले रही थी। इंग्लैंड के गाँव वालों ने देखा कि जिन ग्वालिनों को काउपॉक्स हो जाता है, जो गायों से लगने वाली एक हल्की बीमारी है, उन्हें चेचक नहीं होती लगती।

1796 में एडवर्ड जेनर नाम के एक डॉक्टर ने इसे परखा। उन्होंने सारा नेल्म्स नाम की एक ग्वालिन के हाथ पर काउपॉक्स के फफोले से पदार्थ लिया और आठ साल के लड़के जेम्स फ़िप्स की बाँह पर खरोंचकर लगा दिया। बाद में उन्होंने जेम्स को चेचक के संपर्क में लाया, और लड़का बीमार नहीं पड़ा। आज किसी बच्चे पर ऐसे प्रयोग की कभी इजाज़त नहीं मिलेगी। पर इसी से पहला [[vaccine|टीका]] बना, जिसका नाम लैटिन में [[@cows-india|गाय]] के लिए शब्द पर रखा गया।

sec.h: एशिया और अफ़्रीका के पुराने तरीके

sec.t:
टीके सबसे अच्छा तब काम करते हैं जब ज़्यादातर लोग लगवाएँ। अगर काफ़ी लोग सुरक्षित हों, तो कीटाणु को फैलने के लिए नए लोग नहीं मिलते, और वह ख़त्म हो जाता है। इससे शिशुओं और उन लोगों की भी रक्षा होती है जो इतने बीमार हैं कि टीका नहीं लगवा सकते। इसे झुंड की सुरक्षा, या हर्ड इम्युनिटी, कहते हैं।

दुनिया भर की टीका मुहिम के बाद 1980 में घोषणा हुई कि [[@smallpox|चेचक]] धरती से मिट चुकी है। यह अकेली इंसानी बीमारी है जिसका पूरी तरह सफ़ाया हुआ। पोलियो के साथ भी भारत इसके क़रीब पहुँचा। पल्स पोलियो अभियानों में लाखों स्वयंसेवकों ने पाँच साल से छोटे बच्चों को घर-घर जाकर, ट्रेनों में और बस अड्डों पर दो बूँदें पिलाईं। भारत में जंगली [[@polio-india|पोलियो]] का आख़िरी मामला जनवरी 2011 में पश्चिम बंगाल की एक बच्ची का था।

वैज्ञानिक प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र को कीटाणु दिखाने के [[@future-medicine|नए-नए तरीके खोजते रहते हैं]]। कोविड-19 [[pandemic|महामारी]] के दौरान कुछ शुरुआती टीकों में mRNA का इस्तेमाल हुआ। यह निर्देशों का एक सेट है, जो तुम्हारी कोशिकाओं को थोड़ी देर के लिए वायरस के खोल का एक बेनुकसान टुकड़ा बनाने को कहता है। शरीर उससे सीख लेता है, और निर्देश कुछ ही दिनों में टूटकर ख़त्म हो जाते हैं।

किसी भी दवा की तरह, टीकों के भी साइड इफ़ेक्ट हो सकते हैं, आमतौर पर बाँह में दर्द या एक दिन का हल्का [[@fever|बुख़ार]]। गंभीर प्रतिक्रियाएँ दुर्लभ हैं, और डॉक्टर उन पर बारीकी से नज़र रखते हैं। भारत में सरकार का सार्वभौमिक टीकाकरण कार्यक्रम बच्चों को लगभग दर्जन भर बीमारियों के मुफ़्त टीके देता है। फ़्लू का टीका हर साल बदलता है, क्योंकि फ़्लू के वायरस अपना खोल बदलते रहते हैं।

text: Walking robots balance a lot like we do. They constantly measure how their body is tilting and moving, then shift where they place their feet to stay upright. A tilt [[sensor|sensor]], cameras and sensors in each joint feed a computer, which works out hundreds of times a second where each foot should go next.

Four-legged robots, often called robot dogs, are easier to balance than two-legged ones. With four legs, they can keep three on the ground while one moves, like a tripod. To move quickly, though, they trot with only two feet down at a time, and then they must keep catching their own fall, just as a running animal does.

st.prompt: Which sensor does a walking robot rely on most to know if it is tipping over?

options.t: A tilt-and-turn sensor called an IMU
A microphone listening for falling sounds
A thermometer in each leg

st.reveal: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) contains tiny gyroscopes and accelerometers that measure how the robot's body is tilting, turning and speeding up, hundreds of times a second. It does a job similar to the balance organs in your inner ear.

src: Boston Dynamics, Spot product information.

d.try: Stand on one foot with your eyes open and count how long you can stay steady. Then try with your eyes closed. Most people wobble much more. Your brain mixes signals from your eyes, inner ears and feet to balance, and walking robots also mix cameras, tilt sensors and leg sensors.
myth: Walking robots keep their balance by holding perfectly still and stiff.
Good walking robots balance by moving all the time. Like people, they make constant tiny adjustments, shifting where they put their feet to stay under their body as it tips.

sec.t:
You have a balance organ in each inner ear: tiny loops filled with fluid that sloshes when your head moves. Your brain uses it, along with your eyes and the feel of your feet, to stay upright.

A walking robot has something similar called an IMU, or inertial measurement unit. It is a small chip with gyroscopes, which sense turning, and accelerometers, which sense speeding up and the pull of [[gravity|gravity]]. Motors in each joint also report the angle of the leg and how hard it is pushing. Cameras, and often laser scanners, show the ground ahead, so the robot can spot a step or a hole before it gets there. All of this happens without the robot "thinking" about it in words, much as you don't think about which muscles to tighten when a bus brakes suddenly.

Writing exact rules for every rock, slope and slippery floor is almost impossible. So many teams now let robots learn. They build a computer simulation of the robot and set thousands of virtual copies walking over virtual hills, stairs and ice. Each copy gets rewards for staying upright and moving forward, and slowly improves through trial and error.

Training that would take years in the real world takes hours on fast computers. The lessons are then loaded into the real robot. In 2022, researchers at ETH Zurich in Switzerland used this method to train their four-legged robot, ANYmal. It then hiked up a forested Swiss mountain trail, over roots, mud and loose stones, slightly faster than the time suggested for human walkers.

Boston Dynamics began selling its robot dog, Spot, in 2020. Companies use it to inspect factories, oil rigs and power stations, reading dials and spotting leaks in places that are dangerous or dull for people. In 2022, a Spot robot began patrolling the ancient ruins of [[@pompeii|Pompeii]] in Italy, checking tunnels for damage and signs of illegal digging. Cheaper robot dogs from companies such as China's Unitree are now used in schools and labs.

In 2024, the Indian Army took delivery of 100 four-legged robotic "mules" that can carry supplies and keep watch in the mountains, where real [[@donkeys-mules|mules]] have worked for centuries. Two-legged [[@robots|robots]] are harder. Honda's ASIMO walked and climbed stairs from 2000 until it retired in 2022, and new humanoids now try to walk the way people do.

text: Vande Bharat is a family of fast, modern express trains built in India. The first one ran from New Delhi to [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] in February 2019. More than a hundred Vande Bharat services were running by 2025, linking big cities across the country, usually on day trips of up to about eight to ten hours.

What makes them different is how they move. Most Indian trains are pulled by a locomotive, a separate engine at the front. A Vande Bharat has no locomotive. Instead, electric motors sit under many of the coaches. The whole train pulls itself along, which lets it speed up and slow down much faster.

st.prompt: Vande Bharat trains are designed for 180 km/h. Why do most of them average much less than that on a journey?

options.t: The tracks, curves and signals on many routes don't allow higher speeds
The motors overheat above 100 km/h
The law says passenger trains must go slowly

st.reveal: A train can only go as fast as its track allows. Many Indian routes have curves, level crossings and slower trains sharing the line, so even a fast train often runs at 100 km/h or less for long stretches.

src: Ministry of Railways, Government of India, Vande Bharat Express.

d.try: Find the timetable for any Vande Bharat route on a railway website or app. Divide the distance by the travel time to get the average speed. Then do the same for an ordinary express train on the same route and compare.
myth: Vande Bharat trains zoom along at 180 km/h for their whole journey.

The trains can reach 180 km/h in tests, but in service the top permitted speed is 160 km/h, and only on a few upgraded stretches. Average speeds on most routes are much lower, because the tracks set the limit.

sec.t:
The first train was built at the Integral Coach Factory in [[@chennai|Chennai]], which has made railway coaches since 1955. It was called Train 18, because the plan was to finish it in 2018. A team of Indian engineers designed and built it in about 18 months, and it cost much less than buying a similar train from abroad. Factories in other cities have since joined in, so new trains can roll out faster.

The train was renamed Vande Bharat, meaning "salute to India", before its first trip. Newer versions have been improved again and again, with stronger noses, better seats and more safety features.

Passengers board through automatic sliding doors, and the coaches are sealed and air-conditioned. Every seat has a charging point. Executive-class seats can rotate to face the direction the train is going. Screens show the next station, and the coaches have CCTV cameras.

Many of the trains are fitted for Kavach, an Indian-made system that can brake a train automatically if the driver misses a red signal. It only works where the track has Kavach equipment too, and that is being added route by route.

On test runs, the first Vande Bharat reached 180 km/h. In service, though, the highest speed allowed is 160 km/h, and only on a few upgraded stretches near Delhi. On many routes it [[@averages|averages]] well under 100 km/h, because [[@indian-railways|India's railways]] still have curves, crossings and slower trains on the same lines.

The trains have also faced practical troubles. In 2022, several had their front noses damaged after hitting cattle that wandered onto the tracks. Railways strengthened the design and added fencing on some routes.

A sleeper version, with beds for overnight journeys, began carrying passengers between Howrah and Guwahati in January 2026, so people can travel between distant cities while they sleep. True [[@bullet-trains|bullet trains]], on special tracks, are a separate project. Vande Bharat is about getting faster on the railway India already has.

text: The United Nations, or UN, is an organisation that nearly every country in the world belongs to. It was set up in 1945, at the end of the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. Its job is to help countries settle arguments without fighting, protect human rights and work together on problems like hunger and disease.

Its founders had just lived through two world wars in thirty years. They wanted a permanent place where countries could meet, talk, and act together. Today 193 countries are members. The UN has not ended wars, but it has helped stop some, fed millions of people and vaccinated millions of children.

st.prompt: In the UN Security Council, five countries have a special power called the veto. What does it let them do?

options.t: Block any major decision with a single "no"
Choose the UN's Secretary-General alone
Vote twice on every question

st.reveal: China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA can each stop the Security Council from acting, even if every other member agrees. This was meant to keep the big powers inside the UN, but it also means the Council is often stuck.

d.try: Hold a mini UN in your class or family. Give each person a country, pick a problem such as a shared playground, and give everyone one vote. Then try it again where two people have a veto. Talk about which way felt fairer and which got things done.
myth: The United Nations is a world government that can make laws for every country.

The UN has no power to make laws inside countries. It works mostly through agreement. Only the Security Council can make decisions that members are required to follow, and even those are often hard to enforce.
facts: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish

sec.t:
After the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], countries created the League of Nations to keep the peace. It failed. The USA never joined, and the League could not stop Germany, Italy or Japan from invading other countries.

During the Second World War, the Allies planned something stronger. In 1945, delegates from 50 countries met in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] and signed the UN Charter, the organisation's rulebook. Poland signed soon after, making 51 founding members. India was one of them, two years before it became independent.

The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945. That date is now celebrated as United Nations Day.

Every member country has a seat and one vote in the General Assembly, whether it is as big as India or as small as [[@extreme-smallest-countries|Tuvalu]]. The Assembly meets in New York each September, and world leaders give speeches there.

The Security Council has 15 members and deals with threats to peace. Five of them are permanent: China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA, the main winners of the war in 1945. Each has a [[veto|veto]]. India and several other countries argue the Council should change to reflect today's world, and this debate continues.

The Secretary-General runs the UN's day-to-day work, from the headquarters beside the East River in [[@new-york|New York]].

On 10 December 1948, the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, a list of rights belonging to every person. The Indian delegate Hansa Mehta argued that saying "all men" would leave women out, and the wording was changed to "all human beings".

In 1953, Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit of India became the first woman to lead the General Assembly. Over the decades, India has also sent more than two lakh soldiers and police to serve as UN [[@peacekeepers|peacekeepers]], among the most of any country. Peacekeepers wear blue helmets so they can be recognised.

Critics say the UN is slow, expensive and often blocked by the veto. It failed to prevent terrible events in places such as Rwanda in 1994. Supporters reply that it has helped end several conflicts, wiped out [[@smallpox|smallpox]] through the WHO, and given small countries a voice they would not otherwise have.

The UN and its agencies have won the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] several times. Outside the headquarters, the flags of all member countries fly in a long line, in alphabetical order.

text: By the United Nations' newest count, published in November 2025, the city with the most people is Jakarta in Indonesia, with about 42 million. That's more people than live in all of Canada. Second is Dhaka in Bangladesh, with about 37 million, and third is [[@tokyo|Tokyo]], with about 33 million.

India has two cities in the top ten. [[@delhi|Delhi]] is fourth with about 30 million, more than the whole of Australia, and [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] is ninth with about 22 million. Cairo, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Manila and Seoul fill the other spots.

st.prompt: According to the UN's 2025 count, which city has the most people?

options.t: Jakarta, Indonesia
Tokyo, Japan
New York, USA

st.reveal: Jakarta came first with about 42 million people, followed by Dhaka in Bangladesh. Tokyo, which had topped the list for decades, dropped to third, partly because Japan's population is shrinking and partly because the UN changed how it measures cities.

src: United Nations, World Urbanization Prospects 2025.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, articles on Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo.
n.certNote: The ranking depends on where you draw a city's edge. These figures use the UN's 2025 method, which counts every crowded square kilometre that joins up, and other methods give a different order.

d.try: Look at a map of your own town or city and try to draw its edge with a pencil. Is the edge where the buildings stop, where the city council's area ends, or where people still travel in every day for work? Ask two family members and compare. Each line gives a different population, which is exactly the argument experts have.
myth: Everyone agrees on a single list of the world's biggest cities.

Lists disagree a lot, because some count only the area inside official city limits, some count the whole region people commute from, and the UN now counts joined-up crowded land. Tokyo can be first, third or lower depending on the method.
facts: Dhaka, about 3.7 crore; Tokyo, about 3.3 crore

sec.t:
Dhaka is one of the most crowded places on Earth. Every year, families arrive from villages hit by floods and river [[erosion|erosion]], looking for work in the garment factories. Lagos, Kinshasa and Karachi are also growing very fast.

Tokyo is going the other way. Japan has more deaths than births each year, so the country is shrinking, and its capital is now growing only slowly. Cities rise and fall with the people who move to them.

About 2,000 years ago, ancient Rome may have held around a million people, an enormous number for its time. After Rome shrank, no city in Europe got that big again for well over a thousand years. Around 1800, Beijing was probably the largest city anywhere. London took over during the 1800s, pulled up by factories and trade.

In 1950, only two cities on Earth had 10 million people or more: New York and Tokyo. These giants are called megacities. By 2025 the UN counted 33 of them, and most are in Asia. The UN also found that about 45 percent of all people now live in cities, with many more in towns.

Delhi has grown from under 20 lakh people around 1950 into one of the world's biggest urban areas, drawing people from across the country for work and study. Kolkata, once the capital of British India, has been a giant city for well over a century.

Mumbai isn't in the UN's new top ten, but it's still one of the most crowded cities on Earth, squeezed onto a narrow [[peninsula|peninsula]] with the sea on three sides. Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai are among India's fastest-growing cities.

Counting all these people is a huge job. India is supposed to hold a [[@census|census]] every ten years. The last one took place in 2011, and the next is planned for 2027.

Huge size brings huge problems. Jakarta is sinking. People pumped so much water from under the ground that parts of the city drop several centimetres every year, and some areas sit below sea level. Indonesia is building a new capital, Nusantara, on the island of Borneo, partly because of this.

Big cities also need water, buses, schools, toilets and clean air for millions at once, which is why [[@urban-planning|urban planning]] matters so much. And the strangest part? Jakarta isn't alone, because several other giant cities are slowly [[@earth-sinking-cities|sinking into the ground]] as well.

text: Loktak Lake, in the hills of Manipur, is the largest freshwater lake in Northeast India. Much of its surface is covered with phumdis, floating islands made of tangled grass, roots, soil and rotting plants. Some are small enough for one person to stand on. Others are huge. The largest join together into a floating national park, Keibul Lamjao, about 40 square kilometres in size.

People live on and around the lake, fishing from wooden boats and building huts on the phumdis. The lake also feeds a [[hydroelectric|hydroelectric]] power project and provides water for farms across the valley.

st.prompt: Why do the sangai deer of Loktak walk with a bouncy, "dancing" step?

options.t: The floating ground under their hooves is soft and springy
They are trained by local people
They are scared of snakes in the grass

st.reveal: Sangai live on phumdis, floating mats of plants and soil that sink a little under each step. They lift their legs high and pick their way carefully, which makes them look as if they are dancing.

d.try: Fill a tub with water and float a thick mat of dry leaves, grass and a sponge tied together with string. Press a toy on it and watch it bob and sink a little. Add more layers and see how much weight it holds before it sinks.
myth: The floating islands of Loktak are made by people, like rafts.

Phumdis form naturally from plants, soil and rotting matter that tangle together over many years. People do shape some of them, cutting them into rings for fish farming or building huts on them, but the islands themselves grow on their own.
facts: about 287 sq km, the largest freshwater lake in Northeast India

sec.t:
A phumdi looks like solid land covered in tall grass. But step on one and it sinks and sways a little, like a waterbed. Most of a phumdi's thickness sits below the water, with only a small part sticking out on top, a bit like an iceberg.

Phumdis can be more than a metre thick. In the dry season, some sink down and touch the lake bed, where their roots soak up [[nutrient|nutrients]]. When the rains come and the water rises, they float up again. This yearly rise and fall keeps them healthy.

From above, parts of Loktak look as if someone drew circles all over it. These are athaphums, rings of phumdi cut and arranged by fishing families. Fish gather inside the rings, sheltered by the plants, and are caught with nets.

Many families live in phumshongs, small huts built on floating islands. Children paddle boats to school, and fishers spend days on the water. Life here follows the lake, much like many other [[@people-fishing-villages|fishing villages]] across India. Loktak's fish, plants and snails feed thousands of people around it.

In 1983, the Ithai barrage was built where water leaves the lake, to keep water levels steady for a [[@dams-power|hydroelectric dam]] project. It made electricity, but it also stopped the natural rise and fall of the water.

Without that seasonal dip, many phumdis stopped touching the lake bed. They grew thinner and weaker. In Keibul Lamjao, thin phumdis can sink under the deer's weight, and their grassland is shrinking. Too many phumdis in other parts of the lake block boats and choke the water.

Loktak was named a Ramsar [[wetland|wetland]] of international importance in 1990, and in 1993 it was put on a list of Ramsar sites under threat. Scientists and the Manipur government are trying to balance power, fishing and wildlife. Ideas include opening the barrage gates at certain times to let the water rise and fall again, and clearing phumdis from the open parts of the lake. Some scientists also want a second home for the sangai elsewhere, so that one bad flood can't wipe out the whole [[species|species]].

Loktak is among the great [[@wetlands|wetlands]] of Asia. And it isn't the only strange landscape in [[@northeast-india|India's Northeast]]: a few hundred kilometres away in Meghalaya, people grow bridges out of living tree roots.

text: [[@meghalaya|Mawsynram]] is a village in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in north-east India. It gets about 11,800 mm of rain in an average year. Most lists of [[@world-records|world records]] call it the wettest place on Earth.

The reason is geography. Each summer, the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds blow north from the Bay of Bengal, full of moisture picked up over the warm sea. They cross the flat plains of Bangladesh, where nothing stops them. Then they slam into the steep southern edge of the Khasi Hills. The air is forced upwards, cools, and drops its water as rain, again and again. Mawsynram sits in just the right spot to catch it.

st.prompt: Mawsynram gets about 11,800 mm of rain a year. If it all stayed where it fell, about how deep would it be?

options.t: About 12 m, as tall as a three- or four-storey building
About 1 m, up to your waist
About 100 m, as tall as a skyscraper

st.reveal: Rainfall is measured as a depth. 11,800 mm is 11.8 m. Mumbai, which feels very rainy, gets about 2,200 mm a year, so Mawsynram gets more than five times as much.

src: India Meteorological Department, rainfall records for Meghalaya.
Guinness World Records, wettest place (average annual rainfall).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Cherrapunji.
n.certNote: Mawsynram is usually listed as the wettest place by average yearly rainfall, with nearby Cherrapunji close behind. Lloró in Colombia sometimes claims the title, but its records are less complete, so experts disagree.

myth: Cherrapunji is the wettest place on Earth.
Cherrapunji holds records for the most rain in one year and one month, but in most long-term averages nearby Mawsynram gets a little more. Both are among the very wettest places on the planet.

sec.t:
[[@india-wonder-cherrapunji|Cherrapunji]], also called Sohra, is about 15 km east of Mawsynram. For many years it was known as the wettest place on Earth, and it still holds two [[@weather-records|world records]]. Between August 1860 and July 1861, it received about 26,000 mm of rain, the most ever recorded in a single year. In July 1861 alone it got about 9,300 mm.

In long-term averages, though, Mawsynram usually edges ahead. Lloró, a town in the rainforest of Colombia, has also claimed the title, but its records are not as complete. So the crown is shared and argued over, which is why many books call Mawsynram and Cherrapunji the two wettest places on Earth.

People in the Khasi Hills have adapted cleverly. During the heaviest rains, some farmers wear a "knup", a full-body shield woven from [[@bamboo|bamboo]] and leaves, shaped like a turtle shell. It keeps the rain off while leaving both hands free for work.

Houses have sloping roofs, and some have tin roofs lined with grass to soften the drumming of rain. People dry clothes over fires indoors, and markets keep running whatever the weather.

The Khasi and Jaintia people grow bridges. They guide the roots of the Indian rubber tree, a cousin of the [[@banyan|banyan]], across streams, using bamboo frames to direct them. Over 15 years or more, the roots thicken and twist together into a strong, living bridge.

Some bridges are thought to be centuries old, and they get stronger as they grow. A famous "double-decker" bridge at Nongriat has two levels of roots, one above the other. Unlike wooden bridges, which rot in the constant damp, living bridges love the rain.

Strangely, Cherrapunji and nearby towns can run short of drinking water in winter. Most of the rain falls in just a few months. The steep slopes and thin soil, worn away by years of tree cutting, let water rush straight downhill into Bangladesh instead of soaking in.

Communities are now planting trees, building tanks and protecting springs. In the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]], where water stays can matter as much as how much falls.

text: In Mumbai, many people like to eat [[@lunch-world|lunch cooked at home]], even when they work across the city. So every morning, a dabbawala collects a metal lunchbox, called a *dabba* or tiffin, from a family's door. By lunchtime it is on an office desk, still warm. In the afternoon the empty box travels all the way back.

Before 2020, about 5,000 dabbawalas moved up to 2 lakh lunchboxes a day. In 2026 there were about 3,000, carrying more than 50,000 boxes a day. They do it with [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]], wooden handcarts and the city's crowded [[@indian-railways|local trains]], and with a simple painted code instead of computers.

st.prompt: Most dabbawalas don't use phones, computers or written addresses to sort lunchboxes. What do they use?

options.t: Coloured marks and letters painted on each box
The name of the person written on the lid
A different shaped box for every office

st.reveal: Each lunchbox carries a short code of colours, numbers and letters. It tells the team which station it starts from, which station it goes to, the building and even the floor.

src: Nutan Mumbai Tiffin Box Suppliers Charity Trust, history of the dabbawalas.

n.certNote: The system is real and famously reliable. The often-quoted figure of one mistake in 16 million deliveries comes from a 1998 magazine report and has never been properly measured.

d.try: Make your own dabba code. Pick a colour for your home street, a letter for your school and a number for your classroom. Paint or draw the code on a lunchbox lid, then ask a friend to work out where it is going without telling them.
myth: The dabbawalas make one mistake in every 16 million deliveries.
Nobody has carefully counted. The number came from a magazine in 1998 and stuck. What we do know is that mistakes are rare enough for businesses around the world to study the system.

sec.h: A relay race across the city

sec.t:
Each lunchbox lid carries a few painted marks: colours, letters and numbers. Together they say which station the box starts from, which station it goes to, the building, and sometimes the floor. Many dabbawalas never studied much in school, so the code was designed to be read at a glance, not written out in long addresses.

The system has hardly changed in over a hundred years, because it doesn't need to. It's fast, cheap and works even when phones and computers fail.

sec.h: Why not just use an app?
sec.t: Plenty of apps now deliver food in Mumbai. But an app needs riders on motorbikes stuck in traffic, while a dabbawala crate rides a train that runs every few minutes no matter what the roads look like. The boxes cost very little to send, the food is from home, and the empty box comes back the same day. For many families, that still beats ordering in.

The story usually begins in 1890, when Mahadeo Havaji Bachche started delivering lunches to workers in what was then Bombay. Many people travelled long distances to work, there were few canteens, and families wanted their own food. The business grew with the city.

Most dabbawalas come from farming families in villages near [[@pune|Pune]]. Many belong to the Warkari tradition and wear a white cap. They run their work as a [[@cooperatives|cooperative]]: each member is a partner, not an employee, and they share what the group earns.

In 2003, Prince Charles of the UK visited the dabbawalas and later invited two of them to his wedding. Researchers from business schools, including Harvard, have studied them. Companies that deliver parcels with scanners and [[@barcodes|barcodes]] look at the dabbawalas and ask how people with painted lids manage nearly as well.

When offices closed during the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, deliveries stopped almost overnight and many dabbawalas went back to their villages. Some have returned, and some now carry food from restaurants as well as homes. The city has changed, but a home-cooked [[@thali|thali]] packed into a steel tiffin is still worth crossing Mumbai for.
